accuracy.evidence: Checked against the English National Curriculum Year 1 reading comprehension statements (predicting what might happen on the basis of what has been read so far; discussing the significance of the title and events), the Year 3-4 statement (predicting from details stated and implied) and the EYFS Comprehension early learning goal (anticipate key events in stories). Prediction is presented as a reasoned, revisable guess, never as a right-or-wrong fact, which matches how the curriculum frames it.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-reader slips: random guesses with no link to the text (the moon, the dog reads a book), ignoring the title and pictures (title prediction, cover clue sort, Big Snow challenge), treating page count or book size as clues, giving a guess with no reason (Say why step, ice melt mastery item), sticking with the first guess after the story changes (cat-up-a-tree turn, I said it first challenge option), and believing a wrong guess means being bad at reading (turn-the-page prediction and challenge).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpgnext is built on the act of reading on: a book cover whose clues must be separated from non-clues, three-panel picture stories with guess cards, a guess-plus-clue matching round, and a next-page reveal where the learner chooses to keep or change the guess (one round where keeping is right). Highest 6-token overlap with any other flagship lab is 8% (flag_segbox, shared shell code).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing before the text names it: tapping It has 20 pages answers that page numbers do not tell you what happens; dragging He goes to bed onto the beach story names the spade and sun hat clues; picking a red top as the reason for melting asks which clue would make it melt; keeping the sand guess after the rain page says the rain is a new clue. Done messages state the rule only after the task.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: No, just start reading (the cover task shows three real clues in the title and picture), Any idea you like (the moon and bed guesses are rejected because no clue points there), and Yes, I got it wrong (the turn-the-page step treats changing the guess as the skill). The done message reports the prediction back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with shuffled options and a separate message for every wrong option, e.g. saying it first does not make it right, the cat fell asleep is a new clue; how loud you say it does not matter, a good guess has a because; the page number does not tell you what happens. Wrong taps in the lab give the story-specific reason, such as a red top does not make ice cream melt.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation scores Flesch-Kincaid grade 0.6 and the adult text 8.3, inside the family limits of 5.0 and 10.0. Canvas text is short and concrete (He gets a spade, Big rain starts. Splash!), every story is told with a picture plus three to five words, and the word prediction is defined in the first step.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a clue type, the because sentence frame, the check-and-change routine or a named mistake. The explanation is under 1% the same as any other lesson (nearest: Blending Sounds to Read Words), and each step's done message states the specific rule found, such as the title and pictures are clues, the page count is not.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots of every step in dark and light: the cover and its two-column grid of five clue cards fit without clipping, three story panels fit side by side with a picture and a 14 px caption, and answer cards are full width and at least 56 px tall. Each card has a large button twin below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: all four tasks finish with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, and axe-core finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme, with no console errors. Every drag has a labelled button twin (e.g. The clue is: The sun is very hot), and each result is spoken through the live region and the canvas aria-label.

sources: DfE (2013) English programmes of study, Key Stage 1, Year 1 reading comprehension (predicting what might happen on the basis of what has been read so far; discussing the significance of the title and events)
DfE (2013) English programmes of study, Lower Key Stage 2, Years 3-4 (predicting what might happen from details stated and implied)
DfE (2023) Statutory framework for the Early Years Foundation Stage, ELG Comprehension (anticipate, where appropriate, key events in stories)
Education Endowment Foundation (2021) Improving Literacy in Key Stage 1, Recommendation 4: prediction as a comprehension strategy, modelled and checked against the text
